title: ADR-001: Why Kafka Was the Wrong Choice for My Architecture
subtitle: Evaluating distributed append-only logs vs message brokers: Why I rejected Kafka in favor of native Redis Streams.

sections.tldr: Architecture Decision Record (ADR-001): Evaluated Kafka vs Redis Streams for an untrusted code execution sandbox. While Kafka excels at event streaming, its partition-bound ordering caused severe head-of-line blocking on heterogeneous compute jobs (40ms vs 12s). Redis Streams provided sub-millisecond task leasing with 90% lower operational overhead.

items.body:
When software architects evaluate queue technologies, they often begin with throughput metrics: how many millions of messages per second can the broker ingest? In the context of Interleet—our platform evaluating untrusted code submissions—throughput was an irrelevant vanity metric. The defining constraint of our workload was extreme execution time variance.

Consider the distribution of code execution jobs submitted to an online judge:
- A syntax validation pass or an early exit on a trivial input takes 35 to 80 milliseconds.
- A medium-complexity algorithmic solution running across 30 test cases takes 800 to 2,500 milliseconds.
- An adversarial submission containing infinite loops, heavy recursion, or memory-bound allocations runs until it hits our hard container cutoff threshold of 12,000 to 15,000 milliseconds.

When you push a heterogeneous workload into an append-only partitioned log like Apache Kafka, you run head-first into the partition ordering model. In Kafka, messages within a partition are strictly ordered and offsets are committed monotonically. If consumer Worker A picks up Task #101 (a 12-second adversarial submission) and Tasks #102 through #108 (which are 40ms syntax checks) happen to be appended to that same partition, those fast tasks are completely blocked behind the slow execution.

While you can create dozens or hundreds of partitions to increase parallelism, partition count must be pre-allocated. Because task execution duration is fundamentally unpredictable before the code actually executes in a sandbox, you cannot hash tasks into partitions by duration. Inevitably, slow jobs cluster on the same partition and create catastrophic head-of-line blocking for lightweight tasks.
items.heading: The Workload Profile: Heterogeneous Execution Times

items.body:
Beyond message ordering, Kafka's consumer group protocol introduced a dangerous operational failure mode when paired with long-running sandboxed execution.

In Kafka's consumer architecture, every consumer instance in a group must periodically invoke poll() within a configurable timeout defined by max.poll.interval.ms (defaulting to 300,000ms, but typically tuned lower for task systems). If a worker thread is occupied executing a long C++ compilation or running a multi-test suite inside a Docker sandbox, the worker thread cannot return to poll Kafka in a timely fashion.

If max.poll.interval.ms is exceeded, the Kafka group coordinator assumes the worker has crashed. It immediately kicks the consumer out of the group and triggers a cluster-wide group rebalance. During a rebalance:
1. All partition assignments across all active workers are revoked.
2. Every healthy worker halts consumption while partition reassignment takes place.
3. The in-flight task that triggered the timeout is re-assigned to another worker, which starts executing the exact same slow job from scratch, leading to an infinite retry loop.

Tuning max.poll.interval.ms to 60 seconds or delegating execution to background worker threads creates secondary complexity: decoupling poll() from execution requires implementing custom in-memory buffering, backpressure limits, and out-of-band offset tracking. At that point, you are building a task queue on top of an event log, fighting the abstraction rather than benefiting from it.
items.heading: The Consumer Heartbeat & Rebalance Cascade

items.body:
Engineering decisions must account for the physical constraints of the deployment infrastructure. For Interleet, we operated on a lean cloud infrastructure topology where compute resources were dedicated primarily to code evaluation sandboxes.

Operating a resilient Kafka cluster in production requires:
- A minimum of three Kafka broker instances to maintain quorum and partition replication.
- A metadata consensus layer (either three ZooKeeper nodes or a KRaft quorum of controller nodes).
- Significant JVM heap memory allocation (at least 2GB to 4GB per broker), coupled with substantial host operating system PageCache to leverage Kafka's zero-copy disk writes (sendfile syscall).

Running Kafka effectively consumed 6GB to 12GB of RAM and multiple CPU cores simply to keep the messaging infrastructure idling. For an engineering team managing hundreds of concurrent jobs rather than hundreds of thousands of events per second, running a distributed cluster of JVM daemons was an unjustifiable operational overhead.
items.heading: The Operational Footprint and Infrastructure Weight

items.body:
When we evaluated Redis Streams (introduced in Redis 5.0), the architectural alignment was immediate. Redis Streams natively provide consumer groups (XREADGROUP) without coupling message consumption to rigid partition boundaries.

Here is how task leasing functions under Redis Streams:
1. Independent Task Leasing: When an idle worker calls XREADGROUP, Redis delivers the next unread entry from the stream regardless of prior task durations. Worker 1 can evaluate a 12-second job without preventing Worker 2 and Worker 3 from pulling and completing fifty subsequent fast jobs from the exact same stream.
2. The Pending Entries List (PEL): When Redis delivers a stream entry to a consumer, it marks the entry as pending and records it in the stream's Pending Entries List. The PEL tracks the exact message ID, the assigned consumer, and the elapsed time since delivery.
3. Granular Per-Message Acknowledgments: When a worker finishes an evaluation, it issues an explicit XACK command for that specific message ID. There is no monotonic offset constraint; Task #105 can be acknowledged and purged while Task #101 remains pending without stalling stream progression.
items.code:
# ChaosQueue worker lease execution loop
async def run_worker(redis: Redis, worker_id: str, stream_name: str, group_name: str):
    while True:
        # Pull next task from stream with a 2-second block timeout
        entries = await redis.xreadgroup(
            groupname=group_name,
            consumername=worker_id,
            streams={stream_name: ">"},
            count=1,
            block=2000
        )
        if not entries:
            continue
            
        stream, messages = entries[0]
        msg_id, payload = messages[0]
        task_data = json.loads(payload["data"])
        
        try:
            # Execute sandbox container workload
            verdict = await execute_sandbox(task_data)
            # Acknowledge individual task completion
            await redis.xack(stream_name, group_name, msg_id)
        except Exception as e:
            await handle_failure(redis, stream_name, group_name, msg_id, task_data, e)
items.heading: Where Redis Streams Matched the Access Pattern

items.body:
The remaining challenge with Redis Streams was handling unexpected worker crashes. If a worker container crashes due to an out-of-memory error caused by an untrusted submission, the unacknowledged task remains stranded in the PEL.

To guarantee at-least-once delivery, we built an automatic orphan recovery supervisor. The supervisor inspects the PEL using XPENDING to identify tasks whose idle time exceeds our execution lease threshold (e.g., 20,000ms). It executes an atomic Lua script that invokes XCLAIM, transferring the orphaned task to a healthy consumer while incrementing a delivery attempt counter. If a task fails more than four times, it is routed to a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) to prevent poison-pill jobs from looping indefinitely.

Every architectural decision involves trade-offs. By choosing Redis Streams over Kafka, I accepted two specific trade-offs:
1. Memory vs Disk Storage: Redis keeps stream keys in RAM. To prevent unbounded memory expansion, we enforce stream trimming via XADD tasks:interleet MAXLEN ~ 50000. For our task volume, a 50,000-entry buffer occupies roughly 35MB of RAM.
2. Durability Guarantees: Kafka writes to disk with fsync policies and multi-broker synchronous replication. Redis defaults to asynchronous background snapshots or appendfsync everysec. In the event of a catastrophic host power failure, we could theoretically lose up to one second of queued submissions. In our domain, clients automatically retry pending submissions if a TCP connection drops, making this 1-second recovery window vastly preferable to Kafka's operational burden.
items.code:
-- Atomic Lua script for orphan task recovery and DLQ routing
local stream = KEYS[1]
local dlq_stream = KEYS[2]
local group = ARGV[1]
local consumer = ARGV[2]
local min_idle_ms = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local max_retries = tonumber(ARGV[4])

-- Inspect pending entries with idle time exceeding threshold
local pending = redis.call('XPENDING', stream, group, '-', '+', 10)
for _, entry in ipairs(pending) do
    local msg_id = entry[1]
    local idle_time = entry[3]
    local delivery_count = entry[4]
    
    if idle_time >= min_idle_ms then
        if delivery_count >= max_retries then
            -- Route poison-pill task to dead-letter queue
            local msg = redis.call('XRANGE', stream, msg_id, msg_id)
            if #msg > 0 then
                redis.call('XADD', dlq_stream, '*', 'data', msg[1][2][2], 'reason', 'MAX_RETRIES_EXCEEDED')
                redis.call('XACK', stream, group, msg_id)
            end
        else
            -- Reclaim task to healthy consumer
            redis.call('XCLAIM', stream, group, consumer, min_idle_ms, msg_id)
        end
    end
end

title: Building a Self-Hosted Mail Server from Scratch (SMTP, IMAP & POP3)
subtitle: Implementing RFC 5321, RFC 3501, and RFC 1939 from raw TCP sockets with CockroachDB storage and deliverability compliance.
content: Most developers treat email delivery as a problem to be solved with a third-party API key. For Sharexpress, commercial mail APIs quickly collided with severe constraints: restrictive monthly sending quotas, high recurring expenses, and privacy limitations. We chose to build our own mail infrastructure from the socket layer up.

items.heading: Why Commercial Mail APIs Broke for Sharexpress
items.body:
When scaling automated notification pipelines and secure diagnostic delivery for Sharexpress, we initially integrated commercial transactional email APIs (SendGrid, Postmark). Within three months, we collided with two insurmountable architectural constraints.

First was economic scalability: commercial providers charge steep volume tiers for high-frequency transactional payloads. Second was payload flexibility: our automated diagnostic reports regularly contained 15MB to 25MB encrypted diagnostic archives. Third-party HTTP REST endpoints enforced aggressive request body limits (frequently rejecting payloads over 10MB) or added 4-second upload latencies due to base64 JSON payload inflation.

We asked a foundational engineering question: What does it take to implement a production-grade, RFC-compliant email infrastructure from raw TCP sockets up? The answer forced us to confront protocols designed in the early 1980s that still underpin global internet communications.

items.heading: Implementing the SMTP Protocol State Machine (RFC 5321)
items.body:
SMTP is fundamentally a stateful, line-oriented protocol executed over persistent TCP streams. Unlike HTTP where requests are isolated and stateless, an SMTP daemon must maintain connection state across a strict, lockstep dialogue: greeting (EHLO), TLS upgrade (STARTTLS), sender specification (MAIL FROM), recipient validation (RCPT TO), and payload ingestion (DATA).

We engineered our custom SMTP daemon in Python using asyncio stream readers and writers. The critical parsing challenge was handling line-stuffed byte sequences: in RFC 5321, a single period on a line by itself (\r\n.\r\n) terminates the message payload. If a user email legitimately contains a line starting with a period, the protocol requires prepending a second period (line-stuffing). Our streaming parser inspects byte buffers without loading entire 25MB attachments into process memory, keeping daemon resident memory under 35MB per worker.
items.code:
async def handle_smtp_session(reader: asyncio.StreamReader, writer: asyncio.StreamWriter):
    writer.write(b"220 mail.sharexpress.online ESMTP Service Ready\r\n")
    await writer.drain()
    session = {"helo": None, "sender": None, "rcpt": []}
    
    while not reader.at_eof():
        line = await reader.readline()
        if not line: break
        cmd = line[:4].upper()
        
        if cmd == b"EHLO":
            session["helo"] = line[5:].strip().decode()
            writer.write(b"250-mail.sharexpress.online\r\n250-STARTTLS\r\n250 8BITMIME\r\n")
            await writer.drain()
        elif cmd == b"MAIL":
            session["sender"] = parse_address(line)
            writer.write(b"250 2.1.0 Sender OK\r\n")
            await writer.drain()
        elif cmd == b"RCPT":
            session["rcpt"].append(parse_address(line))
            writer.write(b"250 2.1.5 Recipient OK\r\n")
            await writer.drain()
        elif cmd == b"DATA":
            writer.write(b"354 Start mail input; end with <CRLF>.<CRLF>\r\n")
            await writer.drain()
            await stream_message_body(reader, writer, session)

items.heading: Decoupling Envelope Metadata From Binary Storage
items.body:
A classic failure mode in custom mail servers is storing email headers, status flags, and binary MIME bodies in a single database table. Under high inbox volume, multi-megabyte binary blobs cause extreme table bloat, destroy PostgreSQL buffer cache efficiency, and slow down index scans for simple inbox listings.

We partitioned our storage architecture into two tiers:
1. CockroachDB (Distributed SQL): Stores structured envelope metadata, mailbox indexes, user credentials, and message UID sequences. Read/unread flags (\Seen, \Flagged) update with sub-5ms ACID latency across distributed nodes.
2. MinIO S3 Object Storage: When incoming RFC 822 MIME streams are received, the raw message body and attachments are written directly into an encrypted S3 bucket keyed by SHA-256 message hashes. CockroachDB stores only the S3 object locator and cryptographic digest.

items.heading: The Deliverability Gauntlet: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC
items.body:
Writing the TCP socket daemon was only half the challenge; getting commercial mailbox providers (Gmail, Outlook) to accept messages was the true engineering battle. Modern email deliverability is a web of cryptographic trust:

- SPF (Sender Policy Framework): Configured DNS TXT records designating our static IPv4 and IPv6 blocks as authorized outbound relays.
- DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail): Integrated an automated RSA-2048 signing engine. Every outbound email computes canonicalized header hashes (relaxed/relaxed) and signs them using our private key, verified via public keys published at default._domainkey.sharexpress.online.
- FCrDNS (Forward-Confirmed Reverse DNS): Verified that our public IP PTR record resolves to mail.sharexpress.online, and that the A record for mail.sharexpress.online resolves back to the identical IP address. Without strict FCrDNS alignment, major mail providers reject connections before the EHLO handshake completes.

items.heading: Mailbox Access: Implementing IMAP (RFC 3501) vs POP3 (RFC 1939)
items.body:
To allow desktop and mobile email clients to access mailboxes, we implemented dual retrieval protocols. POP3 was straightforward: authenticating the user, listing message UIDs, streaming messages sequentially, and deleting marked items upon QUIT.

IMAP was vastly more complex due to its bidirectional synchronization semantics. RFC 3501 requires maintaining permanent message UIDs across sessions (UIDVALIDITY), tracking mailbox state flags across concurrent connections, and handling partial message body fetches (e.g., fetching only headers for fast mobile sync). We implemented an atomic UID sequence generator in CockroachDB to guarantee consistency across simultaneous desktop and mobile client connections.

title: Incident #002: When a 4GB Node Suffocated Under Concurrent Contest Traffic
subtitle: Post-mortem of a 14-minute production outage during a university coding contest: swap thrashing, kernel OOM cascades, and architectural recovery.
content: At 8:00 PM on a Friday, the countdown clock on our university hackathon portal reached zero. Within 45 seconds, 300 contestants simultaneously loaded problem descriptions, ran test code, and began submitting solutions. At 8:03 PM, the dashboard stopped updating. SSH sessions refused connections with 'Connection timed out', and the cloud console showed CPU utilization pinned at 100%.
overview: Incident #002: A sudden surge of 300 concurrent participants at contest kickoff triggered an unbounded spike in background compilation jobs. The single 4GB node suffered severe swap thrashing, leading the Linux kernel OOM killer to terminate PostgreSQL. The system was recovered via hard reboot after 14 minutes, followed by architectural tier decoupling.

sections.heading: What the Initial Symptoms Revealed
sections.body:
The symptoms arrived all at once. The frontend web client displayed connection error banners, API health check endpoints stopped responding, and all remote SSH attempts hung at the TCP handshake. Cloud hypervisor telemetry indicated that our single 4GB virtual machine had spiked to 100% CPU utilization and 98% memory consumption.

Because SSH was unresponsive, we had to access the node via the cloud provider's out-of-band VNC serial console. Once authenticated, simple commands like ps aux or top took 30 seconds to render. The system was visibly thrashing.

sections.heading: Kernel Autopsy: Page Cache Eviction and Swap Thrashing
sections.body:
Examining dmesg and system logs after emergency recovery revealed the exact cascade:

1. Unbounded Worker Spawning: At contest kickoff, 80 students clicked 'Run Code' within a 15-second window. Each run command spawned an isolated g++ compiler subprocess.
2. Compilers Competing for Physical RAM: Each g++ compilation consumed between 120MB and 280MB of RAM. With 80 concurrent jobs, compiler memory demands exceeded 10GB—far beyond our 4GB physical capacity.
3. Linux Page Cache Eviction: The kernel's memory management subsystem responded by evicting nearly all filesystem page cache to satisfy anonymous memory allocations.
4. Active Swap Thrashing: The kernel began aggressively swapping active process memory to a virtual disk swapfile. Disk I/O wait spiked to 92%, causing kswapd0 to consume 100% of available CPU cycles.
5. The Fatal OOM Killer Invocation: When swap space was exhausted, the kernel invoked select_bad_process(). The algorithm calculated badness scores based on total memory usage. PostgreSQL, which had reserved 1.2GB for its buffer pool, was chosen as the largest target and killed with SIGKILL.

sections.heading: Why Increasing Concurrency Made Things Worse
sections.body:
Before the contest, our load tests had verified that the FastAPI application could handle 1,200 requests per second for static endpoints. We had configured the worker concurrency pools aggressively, believing that higher concurrency was always better.

What we failed to account for was that compute-bound compiler workloads cannot be multiplexed arbitrarily on a 2-core CPU. Increasing the concurrency ceiling simply allowed more g++ processes to enter the ready queue simultaneously, multiplying memory contention and triggering the swap spiral.

sections.heading: Decoupling Compute Workers From Application State
sections.body:
The permanent resolution required splitting our architecture into isolated tiers:

1. Application & State Tier: The primary 4GB node now hosts PostgreSQL, Redis, and the FastAPI gateway exclusively. No compiler or untrusted binary is ever executed on this machine.
2. Stateless Worker Tier: Compilation and code execution jobs were moved to a separate pool of stateless worker nodes.
3. Token-Bucket Concurrency Semaphores: Workers limit concurrent compilation jobs to exactly 2 per physical CPU core using an asynchronous semaphore. Excess jobs remain safely queued in Redis rather than spawning unbounded OS processes.

sections.heading: The Guardrails That Kept Subsequent Contests Stable
sections.body:
We reinforced the operating system kernel with strict tuning parameters:
- vm.swappiness = 10: Reduced aggressive swapping of active process memory.
- vm.overcommit_memory = 2 with vm.overcommit_ratio = 80: Prevented the kernel from overpromising RAM allocations to child processes.
- Memory Watermarking: Configured systemd watchdog timers that shed queued traffic if available system RAM falls below 15%. Subsequent contests completed with zero downtime.

takeaways: Never run compute-heavy compiler jobs on the same node that hosts your primary database.
High concurrency settings are dangerous when workloads are CPU- or memory-bound.
Disk swap thrashing can degrade a system faster than a clean OOM kill.
Limit concurrent execution workers strictly to available CPU cores and physical RAM budgets.

title: Designing Non-Root Sandboxes for Untrusted Code Execution
subtitle: Defense-in-depth isolation for online code evaluation: AST parsing, cgroups v2, and seccomp-bpf syscall filters.
content: When a user submits code to an online judge, they are handing your server an executable payload of unknown intent. A single uncontrolled submission can fork-bomb the kernel, exfiltrate environment variables, or attempt to join a botnet. Here is the step-by-step lifecycle of how we isolate, inspect, and evaluate untrusted code in Interleet.

sections.heading: The Anatomy of an Untrusted Code Submission
sections.body:
In an educational coding platform, students submit code ranging from benign loop mistakes to deliberately hostile payloads. A naive approach of running subprocess.run(["python", user_code]) directly on a server is suicidal. Even standard Docker containers running as root provide insufficient isolation, as container escape vulnerabilities (like runc exploits) regularly demonstrate.

We engineered a defense-in-depth sandbox for Interleet that treats every submitted program as malicious by default.

sections.heading: Static Analysis Before Compilation
sections.body:
Before any compiler or interpreter is invoked, the submission passes through an automated static analysis pipeline. For interpreted languages like Python, we parse the source code into an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) using Python's native ast module.

The AST visitor inspects import statements, attribute access, and function calls. If the code references forbidden modules (such as ctypes, subprocess, os, socket, or pty), or attempts dynamic import obfuscation (__import__ or builtins.getattr), the submission is rejected instantly at zero execution cost.

sections.heading: Enforcing Hard Resource Boundaries With cgroups v2
sections.body:
Static analysis alone is insufficient: compiled languages (C++, Rust) cannot be easily AST-filtered, and Turing-complete languages can construct malicious behavior dynamically.

We use Linux control groups (cgroups v2) to establish unbreakable hardware limits around every container execution:
- Process Limits (pids.max = 32): Completely neutralizes fork bombs (e.g., :(){ :|:& };:).
- Memory Ceilings (memory.max = 256M): Caps total memory usage including heap and stack; exceeding this triggers an immediate SIGKILL recorded as Memory Limit Exceeded (MLE).
- CPU Throttling (cpu.max = "50000 100000"): Assigns exactly 0.5 CPU cores per container execution window.

sections.heading: Seccomp-BPF: Restricting the Syscall Attack Surface
sections.body:
The Linux kernel exposes over 300 system calls. A standard algorithmic problem only requires read, write, exit_group, brk, and mmap. Allowing access to ptrace, socket, reboot, or mount invites kernel exploitation.

We compiled a custom Seccomp-BPF whitelist profile. Any attempt to invoke a disallowed syscall immediately terminates the child process with SIGSYS without granting kernel execution time.

sections.heading: Filesystem Lockdown and Non-Root Execution
sections.body:
Finally, we enforce container runtime isolation:
- Unprivileged User: The container execution user is explicitly mapped to UID/GID 10001:10001 with zero root capabilities (--cap-drop=ALL).
- Read-Only Rootfs: The container root filesystem is mounted strictly read-only (--read-only).
- Ephemeral RAM Storage: Scratch compilation files are written to an in-memory tmpfs mount limited to 64MB that evaporates the moment the container exits.
- Total Network Isolation: Containers execute with --network none, preventing any outbound TCP/UDP traffic or internal network reconnaissance.
sections.code:
# Production Docker sandbox invocation
docker run --rm \
  --network none \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m \
  --user 10001:10001 \
  --cap-drop=ALL \
  --pids-limit 32 \
  --memory 256m \
  --memory-swap 256m \
  --cpus 0.5 \
  --security-opt seccomp=/etc/interleet/seccomp_strict.json \
  sandbox-cpp-runner:latest

title: Why Production RAG Demands More Than Chunk-and-Embed
subtitle: Beyond naive vector search: Layout-aware extraction, hybrid retrieval (HNSW + BM25), and Cross-Encoder reranking.
content: The standard tutorial for Retrieval-Augmented Generation makes the architecture look trivially simple: extract text from a PDF, split it into 500-token chunks, compute embeddings, and query a vector database with cosine similarity. That recipe works fine for basic text articles. When you deploy it against complex technical documentation with multi-column layouts, financial tables, and dense specifications, it fails continuously.

sections.heading: The Destructive Nature of Arbitrary Chunking
sections.body:
In traditional RAG tutorials, documents are split using naive character or token chunkers (e.g. RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter with chunk_size=500). When applied to real-world technical PDFs, this approach destroys structural meaning.

A complex technical table containing electrical tolerances or price schedules gets sliced across chunk boundaries. Chunk A receives the table header without rows; Chunk B receives rows of numerical values without column labels. When an embedding model vectorizes Chunk B, the semantic context is gone. Vector search returns irrelevant chunks, and the LLM produces hallucinations.

sections.heading: Layout-Aware Extraction: Preserving Table Semantics
sections.body:
To solve this, we redesigned our document ingestion pipeline around visual layout analysis. Instead of treating PDFs as raw byte streams of characters, we pass documents through an OCR and layout detection model that identifies bounding boxes for headers, columns, code listings, and tables.

When a table is detected, the extraction engine converts the tabular grid into structured Markdown table representations before chunking. Furthermore, we inject document breadcrumb metadata (e.g., Document > Section 3.2 > Specifications) into the header of every generated chunk, ensuring that semantic hierarchy is preserved inside the embedding vector.

sections.heading: Why Dense Embeddings Miss Keyword Queries
sections.body:
Dense vector embeddings (such as OpenAI text-embedding-3 or BAAI/bge-large) excel at thematic concepts: searching for 'how to make payments' readily matches 'billing configuration'. However, they exhibit a well-known failure mode with exact keyword lookups: error codes (ERR_CONN_REFUSED_404), serial numbers (MK-9021-X), or exact API function names.

To solve this, we implemented Hybrid Search. We store dense 1536-dimensional vectors using pgvector with HNSW indexing, alongside full-text PostgreSQL tsvector columns with BM25 ranking.

sections.heading: Combining Signals With Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
sections.body:
Combining dense vector distance with BM25 lexical scores requires careful normalization, as raw cosine distances and BM25 scores operate on entirely different mathematical scales.

We use Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), an algorithm that evaluates rank positions rather than arbitrary raw scores:
RRF_Score(d) = \sum_{m \in M} \frac{1}{k + rank_m(d)} (with k=60).
sections.code:
-- Hybrid Search using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) in PostgreSQL
WITH semantic_search AS (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY embedding <=> $1) AS rank
  FROM document_chunks
  ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
  LIMIT 40
),
keyword_search AS (
  SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ts_rank(tsv_body, plainto_tsquery('english', $2)) DESC) AS rank
  FROM document_chunks
  WHERE tsv_body @@ plainto_tsquery('english', $2)
  LIMIT 40
)
SELECT COALESCE(s.id, k.id) as chunk_id,
       COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + s.rank), 0.0) +
       COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + k.rank), 0.0) as rrf_score
FROM semantic_search s
FULL OUTER JOIN keyword_search k ON s.id = k.id
ORDER BY rrf_score DESC
LIMIT 20;

sections.heading: Cross-Encoder Neural Reranking
sections.body:
Even with hybrid retrieval, the top candidate chunks may contain irrelevant passages that happened to share keywords. Bi-encoder embedding models compute query and document representations independently, missing subtle semantic interactions.

As a final stage before prompt assembly, we pass the top 20 candidate chunks through a Cross-Encoder reranker (bge-reranker-large). The Cross-Encoder performs joint attention across the query and candidate chunk simultaneously, scoring exact contextual relevance. Our empirical retrieval precision improved by 38% after adding the reranking stage.

title: How Systematic Pattern Recognition Took Me to LeetCode Knight
subtitle: Reaching the top 1.2% globally: Moving beyond passive editorial memorization into structural algorithmic patterns.
content: For months, my approach to data structures and algorithms was brute-force practice: open a problem, struggle for fifteen minutes, look at the discussion tab, copy the editorial solution, and tell myself I had learned it. After solving nearly 200 problems this way, I entered a contest and failed to solve the second question. The realization was stark: memorizing code produces the illusion of competence without genuine problem-solving ability.

sections.heading: The Trap of Editorial Grinding
sections.body:
The most common mistake engineers make when preparing for algorithmic evaluations is treating problems as isolated trivia questions. You solve 150 questions, memorize code snippets, and feel prepared. But during a live contest or whiteboard interview, the problem prompt changes by a single constraint, and memorized patterns collapse.

The root cause is passive recognition: reading an editorial solution and understanding it requires 10% of the cognitive effort required to derive it from first principles under time pressure.

sections.heading: Deconstructing Problems Into 14 Foundational Archetypes
sections.body:
I stopped grinding random questions and spent three weeks categorizing competitive programming problems into 14 underlying structural templates:

1. Two Pointers & Sliding Window: Contiguous array range invariants.
2. Fast & Slow Pointers: Cycle detection and linked list midpoints.
3. Monotonic Stack & Queue: Finding the next greater/smaller element in O(N).
4. State-Space Graph Exploration: BFS for shortest path in unweighted graphs; DFS for connected components.
5. Top-K Heap Elements: Bounded priority queues for stream processing.
6. Binary Search on Answer Space: Monotonic predicate functions f(x) -> bool.
7. Dynamic Programming Over DAGs: Identifying topological subproblem ordering.
8. Disjoint Set Union (DSU): Dynamic connectivity with path compression.

sections.heading: Recognizing State Invariants in Dynamic Programming
sections.body:
Dynamic programming clicked when I stopped thinking of it as 'filling a 2D matrix' and started viewing it as shortest path exploration over a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subproblem states.

Every DP problem breaks down into three questions:
1. What minimal state tuple (e.g., index, remaining_capacity) uniquely identifies a subproblem?
2. What are the valid transitions from state S to state S'?
3. What is the base case, and in what topological order must states be evaluated?

Once state tuples are defined, transitioning from top-down memoization to bottom-up space-optimized arrays becomes mechanical.
sections.code:
# Monotonic stack: Finding next greater element in O(N)
def next_greater_elements(nums: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    n = len(nums)
    result = [-1] * n
    stack = []  # stores indices of unresolved elements
    
    for i in range(n):
        while stack and nums[i] > nums[stack[-1]]:
            prev_idx = stack.pop()
            result[prev_idx] = nums[i]
        stack.append(i)
        
    return result

sections.heading: How Algorithmic Fluency Informs Production Systems Design
sections.body:
The real payoff of mastering algorithmic patterns was not merely achieving the LeetCode Knight badge (top 1.2% globally with a 1,940+ rating); it was how these concepts transformed my backend engineering.

- Monotonic stacks directly parallel sliding-window rate limiters and log compaction buffers.
- Disjoint Set Union (DSU) informs distributed cluster partition merging and network topology discovery.
- Binary search over monotonic functions is the exact mathematical foundation behind auto-scaling capacity tuning and database connection pool sizing under variable latency budgets.

title: Incident #001: The Race Condition That Returned Stale Contest Standings
subtitle: Debugging a cache-aside race condition under high concurrency: PostgreSQL MVCC isolation, write-ahead logs, and mutex leasing.
content: At 11:30 PM on a Friday during our university coding contest, contestants started noticing erratic behavior on the live leaderboard. A student would submit code, receive an 'Accepted' verdict on their problem page, and then look at the contest standings only to see their previous 'Wrong Answer' state. Refreshing once showed Accepted; refreshing again five seconds later reverted to Wrong Answer.
overview: Incident #001: Under high concurrent submission volume, our Cache-Aside invalidation pattern triggered a race condition. Redis keys were invalidated before open PostgreSQL write transactions committed, allowing concurrent read queries to repopulate Redis with pre-mutation snapshots. Resolved via Transactional Outbox and distributed mutex leases.

sections.heading: When Correct Verdicts Reverted on Refresh
sections.body:
During the final thirty minutes of our flagship programming contest, submission velocity tripled. Students submitted solutions, background worker containers evaluated their code, and PostgreSQL reliably stored the 'Accepted' verdict.

However, the live leaderboard intermittently displayed obsolete scores. A student refreshing their browser would see Accepted, refresh again two seconds later to see Pending, and refresh a third time to see their old score. Some contestants submitted identical code four times thinking the judge had dropped their submission, inflating queue traffic by 400%.

sections.heading: PostgreSQL MVCC Snapshot Isolation Under Concurrent Reads
sections.body:
To understand the bug, you have to trace PostgreSQL's transaction isolation mechanics. Our judge workers ran an ACID database transaction: updating submissions, logging verdicts, and recomputing the student's cumulative score in contest_participants. This multi-row transaction took approximately 120ms under heavy disk I/O.

In our application code, the worker executed:
1. REDIS.DEL("contest:1:leaderboard")
2. db.commit()

While that 120ms commit was still finalizing on disk, twenty concurrent HTTP read requests arrived at the leaderboard API. They found a cache miss in Redis, queried PostgreSQL directly, and received the database snapshot. Under PostgreSQL's default Read Committed isolation level, read queries only observe data committed before the query began. They saw the database as it existed BEFORE the open write transaction finished.

sections.heading: The Fatal Timing of Cache-Aside Invalidation
sections.body:
One of those concurrent read handlers took 140ms to assemble the leaderboard JSON and executed:
REDIS.SET("contest:1:leaderboard", stale_json, ex=600)

Because this SET command finished milliseconds AFTER the write worker's DEL command, the obsolete snapshot was written back into Redis with a 10-minute time-to-live. Every contestant was now served stale data until another write occurred.

sections.heading: Moving Cache Invalidation Into the Write-Ahead Log
sections.body:
To permanently eliminate read-after-write inconsistencies, we overhauled our caching strategy:

1. Transactional Outbox: We removed manual REDIS.DEL calls from API route handlers entirely. Every score mutation writes an invalidation record to an outbox_events table inside the exact same database transaction.
2. WAL-Driven Invalidation: A lightweight background listener tails the PostgreSQL write-ahead log (WAL) and publishes Redis invalidations strictly AFTER the transaction commits to disk.

sections.heading: Lease Locks and Monotonic Version Epochs
sections.body:
To protect against cache stampedes, we introduced distributed mutex leases using Redis:
SET lock:contest:1:leaderboard token NX EX 2

When a cache miss occurs, only the single worker that acquires the lease is permitted to query PostgreSQL. All other concurrent requests wait 50ms and re-check Redis. Furthermore, every cached payload now carries a monotonic version epoch; an atomic Lua script verifies that incoming cache updates never overwrite newer epochs with stale snapshots.
sections.code:
-- Atomic version-guarded cache update script
local current_version = redis.call('HGET', KEYS[1], 'version')
local new_version = tonumber(ARGV[1])

if not current_version or new_version > tonumber(current_version) then
    redis.call('HMSET', KEYS[1], 'data', ARGV[2], 'version', new_version)
    redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], ARGV[3])
    return 1
else
    return 0 -- Rejected: incoming write is stale
end

takeaways: Never execute cache invalidations outside or before the database transaction commits to disk.
PostgreSQL Read Committed isolation means concurrent reads legitimately observe pre-commit snapshots.
Use distributed mutex leases on cache misses to prevent database stampedes during high-traffic moments.
Attach monotonic version epochs to cached payloads to mathematically prevent stale read overwrites.

title: Architecting 25+ Production APIs in FastAPI: Latency & Concurrency
subtitle: Engineering high-throughput Python microservices: Event loop scheduling, connection pool sizing, and zero-allocation auth.
content: FastAPI makes building asynchronous web services straightforward, but the framework's simplicity often hides critical concurrency traps. When developers assume that adding async def to every route handler automatically delivers high concurrency, they are frequently surprised when a single synchronous call brings the entire application's event loop to a halt.

sections.heading: The Single-Threaded Event Loop Bottleneck
sections.body:
Python's asyncio runs a cooperative multitasking event loop on a single operating system thread. When you declare an endpoint with async def, FastAPI executes that coroutine directly on the event loop thread.

If that handler executes a synchronous operation—such as reading a file from disk, calling a legacy synchronous library, or computing an intensive bcrypt hash—the entire event loop freezes. Every other concurrent user request waiting on network I/O is blocked until that single CPU operation completes.

sections.heading: Isolating Blocking Workloads With AnyIO Worker Pools
sections.body:
To maintain sub-10ms p99 latencies, we enforce a strict architectural boundary between asynchronous I/O and synchronous execution:

1. Pure Async: Endpoints performing non-blocking database queries or Redis calls remain async def.
2. Synchronous CPU/Disk Offloading: Any CPU-bound or synchronous blocking call is offloaded to a threadpool using anyio.to_thread.run_sync or executed in a standard def handler (which FastAPI automatically offloads to an internal threadpool).
sections.code:
from fastapi import FastAPI, Depends
import anyio.to_thread

app = FastAPI()

# Dangerous: Synchronous hashing directly in async def blocks all users!
# async def bad_hash(password: str): return bcrypt.hashpw(...)

# Correct: Offload blocking CPU routines to worker threads
async def secure_hash_password(password: str) -> str:
    return await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(
        lambda: bcrypt.hashpw(password.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt()).decode()
    )

sections.heading: Managing Async Database Connection Pools Under Load
sections.body:
A frequent source of microservice degradation is improper database connection pool sizing. When traffic surges, route handlers acquire connections faster than PostgreSQL can service them, resulting in PoolTimeout errors.

We configure SQLAlchemy's AsyncEngine with explicit parameters:
- pool_size = 20: Persistent open connections matching available PostgreSQL worker processes.
- max_overflow = 10: Temporary connections permitted during sudden bursts.
- pool_pre_ping = True: Emits a lightweight SELECT 1 before handing a connection to a coroutine, transparently recycling connections dropped by firewalls or cloud load balancers.

sections.heading: Zero-Allocation Authorization Dependencies
sections.body:
In microservice architectures, verifying permissions on every request can introduce significant latency if route dependencies query the database repeatedly.

We engineered stateless, zero-allocation authorization dependencies. Cryptographic JWT access tokens embed user permissions, tenant scopes, and role hierarchies directly inside the token payload. Route dependencies validate the cryptographic signature and extract claims in-memory in under 0.15ms, completely eliminating database lookups on authenticated read paths.

title: Building ChaosQueue: A Lean Native Async Task Engine From Scratch
subtitle: Guaranteed at-least-once task delivery without Celery: Redis Streams, Lua state machines, and orphan worker recovery.
content: When building asynchronous task pipelines for our internal services, Celery was our initial default. Over several months, Celery proved to be a constant source of friction: complex configuration, heavy third-party dependencies, and opaque failure states when workers disconnected ungracefully. We set out to build ChaosQueue—a minimal, zero-dependency async task queue engineered specifically around native Redis Streams.

sections.heading: The Operational Weight of Celery
sections.body:
Celery is a venerable Python project, but its flexibility comes with significant architectural weight. To support multiple brokers (RabbitMQ, Redis, SQS) and multiple result backends, it introduces an extensive dependency tree (Kombu, Billiard, Vine) and complex multi-process prefork concurrency models.

In containerized cloud environments, Celery workers frequently hung during graceful SIGTERM shutdowns, leaked memory under long-running tasks, and failed to recover unacknowledged tasks cleanly when nodes were preempted.

sections.heading: Why Simple Redis Lists Fall Short
sections.body:
Developers attempting to replace Celery often reach for Redis lists using LPUSH and RPOP. While intuitive, primitive lists lack resilience:

If a worker pops a task with RPOP and crashes a millisecond later, that task is lost forever. While BRPOPLPUSH transfers the task to a processing list, tracking worker heartbeats, managing consumer groups, and handling exponential backoff requires re-inventing a message broker.

sections.heading: Designing Atomic Task Claiming via Lua
sections.body: We built ChaosQueue around Redis Streams and consumer groups. To ensure atomic task dispatching, workers execute an atomic Lua script that claims available tasks and updates in-memory lease timestamps in a single atomic operation inside Redis.
sections.code:
# ChaosQueue worker lease and claim routine
async def consume_next_task(redis: Redis, group: str, consumer: str, stream: str):
    # 1. Claim new task from stream
    entries = await redis.xreadgroup(
        groupname=group,
        consumername=consumer,
        streams={stream: ">"},
        count=1,
        block=1000
    )
    if entries:
        stream_name, messages = entries[0]
        msg_id, payload = messages[0]
        return msg_id, json.loads(payload["data"])
    return None, None

sections.heading: Orphan Task Detection and PEL Recovery
sections.body:
The core reliability mechanism in ChaosQueue is its automatic orphan recovery supervisor. When a worker reads a task via XREADGROUP, Redis registers the task in the stream's Pending Entries List (PEL).

A lightweight supervisor runs an asynchronous loop checking XPENDING. If a task has been pending for longer than its lease threshold (e.g., 30,000ms without an XACK), the supervisor concludes that the worker has crashed. It executes XCLAIM to reassign the task to a healthy worker, ensuring guaranteed at-least-once execution.

sections.heading: Dead-Letter Queues and Exponential Backoff
sections.body:
Tasks that fail due to persistent bugs (poison pills) must not be retried infinitely, as they will starve the worker pool. ChaosQueue tracks delivery retry counts directly in the stream entry metadata.

When a task fails its execution handler, the error counter increments. If retries exceed a configured threshold (default: 5 attempts), ChaosQueue removes the entry via XACK and pushes the failure payload to a quarantine dead-letter queue (DLQ) for forensic analysis.

title: Contributing to Supabase for Google Summer of Code (GSoC 2026)
subtitle: Navigating polyglot distributed architectures: Reproducible Docker environments, regression testing, and upstream collaboration.
content: Opening the Supabase GitHub organization for the first time is humbling. Unlike traditional monolithic open-source projects, Supabase is a distributed orchestration of distinct systems: an authentication service in Go (GoTrue), real-time WebSockets on the Erlang/Elixir BEAM VM, a frontend studio in Next.js, and C-based PostgreSQL extensions. Contributing effectively required a complete shift in development discipline.

sections.heading: Navigating a Polyglot Distributed Architecture
sections.body:
When preparing for Google Summer of Code (GSoC 2026), I chose Supabase because of its open-source backend architecture. However, understanding how the services interact requires tracing distributed request paths:

A client authentication request hits Kong API gateway, routes to GoTrue (written in Go), writes to PostgreSQL, and triggers real-time replication via logical decoding slots to Realtime (written in Elixir). Navigating this codebase taught me how to read systems across four programming languages without getting lost in implementation trivia.

sections.heading: Mastering the Local Multi-Service Development Environment
sections.body:
You cannot make reliable contributions to distributed infrastructure by testing against hosted cloud instances. Mastering the local development toolchain was my first milestone.

Using the Supabase CLI and Docker Compose, I containerized the entire backend stack locally. This enabled rapid iteration on database migrations, custom PostgreSQL extensions, and gateway routing configurations with zero cloud latency and complete offline repeatability.

sections.heading: Writing Reproducible Integration Test Suites
sections.body:
The highest barrier to merging open-source pull requests in infrastructure repositories is test quality. Core maintainers do not have time to debug flaky tests.

I established a disciplined testing workflow: every feature or bugfix includes automated integration tests that spin up fresh PostgreSQL schemas in Docker, execute transactions with intentional network latency or abort signals, and verify that rollbacks cleanly restore database consistency.

sections.heading: The Mechanics of Upstream RFCs and Maintainer Collaboration
sections.body:
The most important lesson from open-source collaboration is that code is the last step of the process. Submitting an unexpected 800-line pull request is the fastest way to get ignored.

I learned to open concise Request for Comments (RFC) issues first:
1. Explaining the architectural trade-off.
2. Demonstrating reproduction benchmarks.
3. Proposing minimal, backward-compatible API designs.
Aligning with maintainers before writing code ensured that pull requests addressed actual roadmap priorities.

title: Turning Local Apple Silicon Into a Distributed Compute Worker Behind NAT
subtitle: Overcoming residential CGNAT with reverse WebSockets to run heavy embedding and evaluation tasks on local Metal GPUs.
content: Running local machine learning models and heavy integration test suites on cloud instances (e.g., AWS EC2 g4dn or c5.xlarge) was costing over $180 every month. Sitting on my desk was an M-series Apple Silicon Mac with 36GB of unified memory and a 16-core Neural Engine that remained idle for hours. The challenge was network topology: my laptop sat behind a residential Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT) with no public IPv4 address and dynamic port assignments.

sections.heading: The Ingress Problem: Why Standard Schedulers Fail
sections.body:
In standard distributed compute clusters (like Kubernetes or Celery with inbound HTTP/gRPC listeners), the central orchestrator requires bidirectional network reachability to dispatch tasks to worker nodes.

When working from a residential ISP or university network, your machine is assigned a private RFC 1918 address behind multiple layers of Carrier-Grade NAT (CGNAT). Inbound connections are blocked by ISP firewalls, and public IP addresses change unpredictably. Port forwarding was impossible, and commercial VPN tunneling tools introduced prohibitive bandwidth latency.

sections.heading: Reverse Tunneling via Outbound Persistent WebSockets
sections.body:
Instead of trying to open inbound ports, we inverted the network topology. The local worker daemon initiates an outbound, TLS-encrypted WebSocket connection (wss://orchestrator.interleet.com/v1/workers/connect) to our central cloud gateway.

Because outbound TCP connections over port 443 are universally permitted by firewalls and NAT gateways, the connection establishes cleanly. Once the WebSocket handshake completes, the full-duplex TCP stream remains open. The cloud orchestrator can dispatch compute tasks downward to the laptop in sub-millisecond time.
sections.code:
# Local compute daemon reverse connection loop
async def connect_worker_tunnel(orchestrator_url: str, secret_token: str):
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {secret_token}", "X-Worker-Capabilities": "metal,docker"}
    async with websockets.connect(orchestrator_url, extra_headers=headers) as ws:
        # Register capabilities with orchestrator
        await ws.send(json.dumps({"type": "REGISTER", "cores": 12, "ram_gb": 36}))
        while True:
            raw_task = await ws.recv()
            task = json.loads(raw_task)
            # Dispatch to local Apple Silicon Metal worker
            result = await execute_on_metal(task)
            await ws.send(json.dumps({"type": "RESULT", "task_id": task["id"], "output": result}))

sections.heading: Dispatching Compute Tasks to Apple Silicon Metal
sections.body:
The local daemon interfaces directly with macOS Metal Performance Shaders (MPS) via PyTorch. For text embeddings and reranking tasks, Apple Silicon's unified memory architecture provides extraordinary throughput: because the CPU and GPU share the same physical RAM bus, zero-copy tensor transfers eliminate the PCIe bottleneck common to discrete desktop GPUs.

We offloaded batch embedding generation for thousands of documents locally, saving hundreds of dollars in cloud compute costs while maintaining sub-50ms inference times.

sections.heading: Heartbeats, Authentication, and Connection Resilience
sections.body:
Laptops are inherently unstable infrastructure: lids close, Wi-Fi connections flap, and machines enter sleep mode. To prevent the cloud orchestrator from dispatching tasks into a dead connection, we implemented:

1. Bidirectional Ping-Pong Heartbeats: Emitted every 10 seconds; missing two consecutive heartbeats marks the worker as offline in Redis.
2. HMAC-SHA256 Challenge Tokens: Prevents unauthorized machines from joining the worker pool.
3. Exponential Backoff Reconnection: Automatically re-establishes the WebSocket tunnel when network connectivity returns.

title: Debugging Event Ordering Anomalies in a Real-Time SSE Pipeline
subtitle: How browser reconnection semantics exposed stateless Pub/Sub gaps, and why we rebuilt real-time events with Redis Streams.
content: When contestants submitted code on our contest platform, the UI displayed a real-time evaluation card showing live progress across 40 test cases: 'Compiling...', 'Running Test Case 12/40...', 'Accepted'. Under standard network conditions, it worked smoothly. But when a contestant experienced momentary Wi-Fi packet loss, the UI went haywire: test case 14 would display before test case 8, and finished submissions would suddenly revert to 'Compiling'.

sections.heading: The Disappearing and Out-of-Order Test Case Verdicts
sections.body:
The bug was reported during live testing: a user on a mobile hotspot submitted a solution, the UI flickered, and suddenly test case #22 appeared as passed while test cases #1 through #21 were still marked as pending. Seconds later, the submission status reverted to 'Queued'.

Frontend developers assumed the React state reducer had a race condition. But when we inspected network packet captures in browser developer tools, the browser was genuinely receiving events out of sequence.

sections.heading: The Flaw in Combining EventSource Reconnection With Redis Pub/Sub
sections.body:
Our original architecture paired HTTP Server-Sent Events (SSE) with Redis Pub/Sub:
1. Contestant submits code.
2. Browser connects to /api/v1/submissions/{id}/stream via EventSource.
3. FastAPI endpoint subscribes to Redis channel submission:{id}:events.
4. Judge worker publishes progress events via REDIS.PUBLISH.

Here was the structural flaw: Redis Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget. It does not buffer or persist messages. When a user experiences a 200ms Wi-Fi blip, the browser's EventSource client automatically closes the dead socket and opens a new HTTP connection. During that reconnection window, any events published to Redis Pub/Sub evaporate into thin air.

sections.heading: Switching to Persistent Redis Streams With Consumer Groups
sections.body:
To guarantee reliable delivery, we replaced ephemeral Redis Pub/Sub with persistent Redis Streams:
Instead of publishing to a channel, the judge worker appends events to a stream keyed by submission ID:
XADD submission:1042:events * step "TEST_CASE" index 12 verdict "PASSED"

When an SSE client connects (or reconnects), the FastAPI endpoint reads from the stream using XREAD starting from the exact Last-Event-ID provided in the browser's HTTP request header. No events are ever missed during connection flapping.

sections.heading: Monotonic Sequence IDs and Client-Side Reconciliation
sections.body:
On the frontend, we hardened the event consumption layer. Every event payload carries a strictly monotonic sequence counter (seq_num: 1, 2, 3...).

The client-side event listener maintains an expected sequence pointer. If an incoming event arrives with a seq_num lower than the highest recorded state, it is discarded as an obsolete frame. If an event arrives with a gap, the client buffers it temporarily until missing sequence frames are replayed. This completely eliminated flickering and out-of-order UI transitions.

title: Database Buffer Profiling and Cache Stampede Mitigation in PostgreSQL
subtitle: Diagnosing 95% CPU spikes under traffic surges: Query optimization with EXPLAIN ANALYZE BUFFERS and probabilistic XFetch caching.
content: When a 2-hour university coding competition ended, our platform experienced a sharp, predictable traffic surge: hundreds of students simultaneously refreshed their dashboards to check final rankings and review submitted solutions. Within sixty seconds, PostgreSQL CPU utilization jumped to 96%, query latencies degraded from 15ms to over 2.4 seconds, and HTTP connection pools began exhausting.

sections.heading: Diagnosing the Database Suffocation
sections.body:
The symptoms were unmistakable: as soon as the contest clock stopped, the API server's connection pool began queuing requests. Application logs filled with pool timeout warnings, and p99 query latencies exploded from 12ms to 2,400ms.

Because our application used Redis caching, we initially assumed Redis had crashed. But Redis was completely healthy, reporting 2% CPU usage and plenty of free memory. The bottleneck was entirely within PostgreSQL.

sections.heading: Profiling Physical Disk and Buffer Access With EXPLAIN ANALYZE BUFFERS
sections.body:
Running standard EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows execution times, but adding the BUFFERS parameter reveals physical memory interactions. We profiled the leaderboard aggregation query:
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT ... FROM submissions WHERE contest_id = 42 ORDER BY score DESC, submission_time ASC;

The output revealed a disaster:
Buffers: shared hit=4210 read=82450
PostgreSQL was performing a sequential table scan across 82,450 shared 8KB buffer blocks (over 650MB of data) for every single leaderboard request. Under 200 concurrent requests, the database was repeatedly thrashing physical disk blocks through memory.

sections.heading: Engineering Composite B-Tree Indexes
sections.body:
The sequential scan occurred because our existing index only covered contest_id. PostgreSQL had to fetch thousands of submission rows from disk and sort them in work_mem.

We created a targeted composite B-Tree index matching the exact query predicate and sort order:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_submissions_contest_score_time ON submissions (contest_id, score DESC, submission_time ASC);

Re-running EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) showed immediate transformation:
Buffers: shared hit=18 read=0
Execution time dropped from 1,840ms to 0.8ms—a 2,300x performance improvement.

sections.heading: The Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd) Phenomenon
sections.body:
Even with optimized queries, serving 500 requests per second directly from PostgreSQL during peak moments is wasteful. However, naive TTL caching introduces cache stampedes:

Suppose key contest:42:leaderboard is cached with a 120-second TTL. For two minutes, all requests are served from Redis in 1ms. At second 121, the key expires. Instantly, all 200 concurrent incoming requests experience a cache miss simultaneously, and all 200 fire the aggregation query at PostgreSQL at the exact same millisecond.

sections.heading: Implementing Probabilistic Early Expiration (XFetch)
sections.body:
To permanently eliminate cache stampedes, we implemented the XFetch algorithm (Vattani et al.). Instead of waiting for a cache key to expire, workers probabilistically recompute the cached value before expiration:

Recompute if: -\beta \times \delta \times \ln(\text{random}()) > \text{TTL}_{\text{remaining}}
Where \beta > 0 (aggressiveness factor), \delta is the computation time, and random() \in (0, 1).

As the key nears expiration, the probability of recomputation smoothly increases. Exactly one worker recomputes and refreshes the cache early while all other concurrent requests continue receiving fast cache hits. Under load testing, cache stampedes were completely eliminated.
sections.code:
import math, random, time

def should_recompute_xfetch(cached_at: float, ttl_seconds: float, delta_seconds: float, beta: float = 1.0) -> bool:
    """
    XFetch Probabilistic Early Expiration Algorithm
    delta_seconds: Time taken to compute the value
    beta: Aggressiveness factor (> 0)
    """
    time_remaining = (cached_at + ttl_seconds) - time.time()
    if time_remaining <= 0:
        return True
    # Probabilistic early recomputation condition
    return (-beta * delta_seconds * math.log(random.random())) > time_remaining
